title: Mara, you are seen
hookLine: Mara comes as an ox, a farmer, a voice of doubt; each time he is recognized (SN 4)
tomorrow: What does being a woman matter

lines: AN OX NEAR THE DRYING BOWLS.
cards: The monks have set their alms bowls out in the open to dry. An ox wanders toward them, big and clumsy. One monk says to another, that ox is going to break the bowls.
Another day, a farmer walks past with a plow on his shoulder and a goad in his hand, asking if anyone's seen his oxen. Another day, there's just a voice, whispering that you're wasting your life.
Same visitor, every time, in a different coat. The Samyutta gives him a whole chapter.

teach.h: MARA: THE ONE WHO KEEPS BEINGS CAUGHT
teach.b: Mara is the tempter in the Buddhist texts, the one who wants beings to stay caught. His name is linked to death, and he's sometimes called the Evil One.
The fourth chapter of the Connected Sayings is all Mara, a run of short scenes with a pattern.

teach.h: AN ELEPHANT, A SERPENT, AN OX, A FARMER
teach.b: Mara shows up, often in disguise: a huge elephant king in the dark, a serpent, the ox by the bowls, a farmer who argues that the eye and the ear and all the senses belong to him.
Sometimes he's just a voice: you're not really awake, why bother, go back to ordinary pleasures.
And every time, the Buddha recognizes him. That's the turn. He doesn't fight, flee, or argue for an hour.
He knows: this is Mara, and often says so in a short verse.

teach.h: THE BLESSED ONE KNOWS ME, AND HE GOES
teach.b: Then comes the line that closes scene after scene, almost a refrain: Mara, realizing the Blessed One knows me, sad and disappointed, disappears right there. Being seen is enough.
Read as psychology, the chapter is strikingly practical. Temptation rarely announces itself. It arrives as something ordinary, a heavy animal, a reasonable farmer, a sensible voice of doubt.
The power lies in the disguise; once it's named, much of that power is gone.
Buddhist schools differ on how literally to take Mara. Some traditional readers take him as a real being, a deity of the desire realm. Some modern teachers read him as a picture of craving and fear.

how: Buddhist art across Asia shows Mara and his armies at the night of the awakening, and some meditation teachers encourage students to name distractions and cravings as they arise, sometimes playfully as visits from Mara.

games.q: you're a monk drying your bowl. an ox wanders toward the bowls, and your teacher says it's Mara in disguise. what does the chapter show as the answer?
o: chase the ox away with a stick.
see it clearly for what it is.
pack up the bowls and leave.
games.why: in scene after scene, recognition is enough: Mara knows he's been seen, and disappears right there.

practice: Think of one temptation that keeps visiting you, the extra scroll, the sharp reply, the voice that says skip it, and picture the disguise it usually wears: tired, reasonable, deserved.
Quietly, or aloud if you're alone, name it in a plain sentence, not angry, not afraid, the way you'd greet an old acquaintance at the door: I see you.
Then let the breath carry on, and notice what happens to the pull once it's been named.

wordCard.voice: Mara. The tempter of the Buddhist texts, whose name means death; in SN 4 he comes in disguise again and again, and each time he is recognized and disappears. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit Mara: the tempter, from a root meaning death, to die or to kill.
